query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating oxygen-impurity-inclusive ab initio data of electron scattering into a physics-informed machine learning model will enable conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr (with ~1 wt.% oxygen) that match experimental values within ±10% over both the cryogenic (0–200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes, outperforming traditional perfect‐crystal analytical models.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy containing inherent point defects, including approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a hybrid, physics-informed machine learning framework that integrates defect‐inclusive ab initio simulation datasets—explicitly capturing oxygen impurity scattering and temperature‐dependent electron–phonon interactions—to parameterize scattering rates.
generation.conditions: The predictions are focused on samples of HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 wt.% oxygen. The model is applied over two temperature regimes: 0–200 K, dominated by impurity (quantum) scattering, and 300–1200 K, where phonon scattering interacts with defect dynamics.
generation.structural_mediator: The spatial distribution and local environment of oxygen impurities, which modify electron scattering rates and thus the effective electronic conductivity of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures (0–200 K), oxygen impurities introduce additional scattering centers, leading to enhanced impurity-driven electron scattering. At high temperatures (300–1200 K), the interaction between oxygen-induced defect scattering and thermally activated phonon scattering further modulates electron transport. The integrated machine learning model accounts for these effects by adjusting scattering rates based on defect concentration and temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The machine learning model is expected to predict temperature-dependent conductivity values that remain within a ±10% error margin of experimental measurements, thereby accurately capturing the crossover from impurity-dominated scattering at cryogenic temperatures to combined phonon and defect scattering at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Traditional analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystal assumptions, which typically overestimate conductivity by neglecting the impact of oxygen impurity scattering.
generation.boundary: The improved prediction accuracy applies specifically to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and within the temperature ranges of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. The model may not be directly applicable to alloys with significantly different oxygen concentrations or to other high-entropy alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: While the ±10% error margin is targeted, uncertainties remain due to potential complexities in defect interactions and possible limitations in the available defect-inclusive datasets.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with a verified oxygen content of ~1 wt.%. Conduct temperature-resolved four-point probe electrical conductivity measurements across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. In parallel, use the developed physics-informed machine learning model to generate conductivity predictions for these specimens. Compare the predicted values against the experimental data and against predictions made by conventional perfect‐crystal models.
measurements: Temperature-resolved electrical conductivity (using four-point probe techniques)
Oxygen content verification via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS)
Structural characterization (using X-ray diffraction, XRD) to confirm phase purity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the physics-informed machine learning model fails to predict the experimental conductivity within a ±10% error margin in either the 0–200 K or 300–1200 K regimes, or if its performance does not show a statistically significant improvement over traditional perfect‐crystal analytical models.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . High-damping alloys are an important family of metallic materials for applications that require noise/vibration reduction, shock absorption, and energy conversion, in structures ranging from large-scale aircrafts to small-sized electrical devices ( [1] ). Traditional alloys used to reduce noise and vibrations achieve their mechanical damping capacity by primarily manipulating crystalline defects or/and interfaces, such as dislocations ( [2] , [3] ), phase or twin boundaries ( [4] – [6] ), and magnetic domain boundaries ( [7] ). However, when exposed to mechanical vibrations and the associated stresses, both crystal defects and interfaces in these conventional alloys tend to rearrange and aggregate. As a result, the whole relaxation process is irreversible and the damping capacity gradually deteriorates ( [1] , [8] ). In addition, these irreversible relaxation processes accelerate when the service temperature increases. This means that structural stability and the high-temperature damping capacity of traditional noise reduction alloys are often insufficient for long-term use ( [8] , [9] ). The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. frame.system: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy, typically modeled as a perfect crystal but in reality containing point defects such as ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities
frame.goal: To formulate a predictive hypothesis that accurately estimates conductivity (or related transport properties) over two temperature regimes (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) by explicitly incorporating defect and impurity effects, thereby overcoming the limitations of ideal, defect‐free analytical models.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical predictions are limited by their reliance on perfect crystalline assumptions, which ignore the influence of defects (such as oxygen inclusion), leading to limited accuracy especially across wide temperature ranges.
root_cause_cues: limited accuracy of available analytical predictions
usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals
constraints: Must address both low temperature (0–200 K) and high temperature (300–1200 K) regimes
Include effects of non-negligible defect concentrations (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen)
Define clear applicability limits in temperature and sample purity
Provide a falsifiable conductivity benchmark with a specific result range
frame.regime: Operating and test conditions span a cryogenic regime (0–200 K) where quantum and impurity scattering may dominate and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) where increased phonon scattering and defect dynamics are active; experiments on specimens with and without 1 wt.% oxygen are available.
prior_attempts: Analytical approaches based on perfect, defect-free crystals using standard band structure or Boltzmann transport methods
Empirical or simplified models that do not account for the complex scattering phenomena introduced by defects or disordered alloying in high entropy systems
frame.understanding: The hypothesis posits that a combined predictive model—potentially incorporating atomistic simulations, defect scattering theory, and machine learning techniques trained on defect-inclusive datasets—will yield enhanced accuracy by explicitly simulating the impact of point defects (e.g., oxygen impurities) on electron transport. This improvement is supported by prior evidence in disordered systems where including defect contributions leads to better predictions of transport properties. Additionally, a benchmark conductivity value (obtained from a held-out experimental dataset) is defined such that if the predictive model’s output deviates beyond an acceptable error margin (e.g., failing to capture the known drop or increase in conductivity within a pre‐specified range), the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Early analytical and simulation studies of high‐entropy alloys, such as those using Boltzmann transport in defect‐free, perfect crystal models, succeeded in capturing trends under idealized conditions but failed to account for the dominant effects of defects (e.g., oxygen impurities) on transport properties. More recent work (e.g., PMC8357793) has started to leverage machine‐learning interatomic potentials and atomistic simulations to capture defect or short‐range order effects in disordered systems, while PMC11077685 directly studies HfNbTaTiZr with evidence that ~1 wt.% oxygen substantially modifies properties (here, via interstitial strengthening). Despite these advances, no study has yet integrated defect‐induced scattering mechanisms into predictive models of conductivity across both the cryogenic (0–200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes.
decision.unsolved: Existing analytical approaches lack incorporation of complex defect (oxygen) and disorder effects that dominate electronic scattering in real HfNbTaTiZr alloys, especially over wide temperature ranges. In particular, capturing the crossover between quantum/impurity-dominated scattering at low temperatures and phonon plus defect dynamics at high temperatures remains unsolved, and quantitative predictions fail without explicitly including these mechanisms. Moreover, the impact of ~1 wt.% oxygen on the electronic transport benchmark (the held-out conductivity value) has yet to be simulated with fidelity.
decision.lever: Integrate defect‐inclusive datasets—synthesized from ab initio calculations that explicitly include oxygen impurity scattering and temperature-dependent electron–phonon interactions—with a physics-informed machine learning framework that allows control of scattering rates as key parameters.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend of incorporating disordered effects via machine learning (as seen in defect‐sensitive studies like PMC8357793) and addresses the failure of idealized, perfect-crystal models by training on data that includes realistic defect configurations (e.g., the oxygen content documented in PMC11077685). By explicitly parameterizing both low-temperature impurity scattering and high-temperature phonon plus defect dynamics, the model should improve predictive accuracy, allow clear definition of temperature and composition limits, and set a strict conductivity benchmark that—if not met (e.g., if the held-out experimental conductivity falls outside a pre‐defined error margin, say ±10% of the measured value)—will falsify the hypothesis.
